_Requirement: Text alternatives must be provided for any non-text content such as images, charts, graphics, and animations. The text should provide equivalent information as the visual element. If non-text content does not communicate information, is purely for decoration, is used only for visual formatting, or is not presented to users, then it should be implemented in a way that it can be ignored by assistive technology (for example, marked as decorative).
_Applicability:
This rule applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface, except for the situations listed below: 

**Controls, Input:** If non-text content is a control or accepts user input, then it has a [name](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-name) that describes its purpose. (Refer to [Success Criterion 4.1.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#name-role-value) for additional requirements for controls and content that accepts user input.) 

**Time-Based Media:** If non-text content is time-based media, then text alternatives at least provide descriptive identification of the non-text content. (Refer to [Guideline 1.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#time-based-media) for additional requirements for media.) 

**Test:** If non-text content is a test or exercise that would be invalid if presented in [text](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-text), then text alternatives at least provide descriptive identification of the non-text content. 

**Sensory:** If non-text content is primarily intended to create a [specific sensory experience](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-specific-sensory-experience), then text alternatives at least provide descriptive identification of the non-text content. 

[CAPTCHA](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-captcha): If the purpose of non-text content is to confirm that content is being accessed by a person rather than a computer, then text alternatives that identify and describe the purpose of the non-text content are provided, and alternative forms of CAPTCHA using output modes for different types of sensory perception are provided to accommodate different disabilities. 

**Decoration, Formatting, Invisible:** If non-text content is [pure decoration](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-pure-decoration), is used only for visual formatting, or is not presented to users, then it is implemented in a way that it can be ignored by [assistive technology](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-assistive-technologies).
_Guidance: MAS 1.1.1 - Non-text Content is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.1.1 Non-text Content - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Non-text Content to 9.1.1.1 web, 10.1.1.1 non-web documents, and 11.1.1.1.1 software.

_DetectionPatterns: Images without text alternatives (no alt attribute, no aria-label, etc.)
Alternative text containing only white space or generic alternative text such as 'image' or the file name of the referenced graphic
Text alternatives that are redundant to text content of the page
Decorative images not properly marked
Complex images without detailed descriptions

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Add descriptive text alternative that conveys the same information as the image
Examples: Chart ? 'Sales increased 40% from Jan to Mar'

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Mark as decorative so assistive technology ignores it
Examples: Visual separators which are not interactive
User avatar image that precedes a username
Graphic element that is a descendent of a link or button that get their accessible name from an aria-label

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Provide brief alternative plus detailed description
Examples: Chart with data table containing the same information

ValidationCriteria: Alternative text conveys equivalent information
Decorative images are properly marked
Complex content has concise alternative text along with a detailed description in another format (e.g., as tabular data or a long text summary)

Good: Logo: Use company or product name as the text alternative
Functional image: Describe the purpose or action/function of the control the image represents
Informative image: Describe key information conveyed
Animation: Summarize key points of the animation or a high level narrative the animation conveys
Bad: Using generic text like 'image', 'graphic', 'screenshot' (without further context), 'logo', 'photo' or the file name of the graphic
Repeating nearby text exactly
Describing appearance instead of meaning

exceptions.description: If non-text content is a control or accepts user input, then it has a an accessible name that describes its purpose

If non-text content is pure decoration, redundant to other text content, used only for visual formatting, or is not intended to be presented to users, implement so it will be ignored by assistive technology

_Requirement: A text transcript or an audio track must be provided for all pre-recorded audio-only content. Captions or a text transcript must be provided for all pre-recorded video-only content.The alternative format should present equivalent information as the pre-recorded content.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to pre-recorded audio-only content and video-only content published by Microsoft, except when the audio or video is a [media alternative for text](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-media-alternative-for-text) and is clearly labeled as such. 
This requirement does not apply to third-party content that Microsoft licenses solely for redistribution, such as content provided via online streaming services.
_Guidance: MAS 1.2.1 - Audio-only and Video-only (Pre-recorded) is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.2.1: Audio-only and Video-only (Pre-recorded) - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Audio-only and Video-only (Pre-recorded) to 9.1.2.1 web, 10.1.2.1 non-web documents, and 11.1.2.1.1 software.

_Requirement: Captions must be provided for all [pre-recorded audio](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-audio "pre-recorded audio") in audiovisual content.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to pre-recorded audio in audiovisual content published by Microsoft.

This requirement does not apply to: 
- Third-party content that Microsoft licenses solely for redistribution, such as content provided via online streaming services.
- Video players – See MAS 7.1, 7.1.4, 7.3, and 7.6 for rules applicable to video players.
- Video creation and editing tools – See MAS 5.x for rules applicable to authoring tools.
_Guidance: MAS 1.2.2 - Captions (Pre-recorded) is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.2.2 Captions (Pre-recorded) - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles to Captions (Pre-recorded) to 9.1.2.2 web, 10.1.2.2 non-web documents, and 11.1.2.2 software.

_Requirement: Captions must be provided for all audiovisual content containing live (real time) audio (for example, live product announcements or teleconferences). Live captions should be synchronized and not obscure on-screen visuals.
_Applicability: This requirement applies to live audio in audiovisual content.
_Guidance: MAS 1.2.4 - Captions (Live) is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.2.4 Captions (Live) - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles to Captions (Pre-recorded) to 9.1.2.2 web, 10.1.2.2 non-web documents, and 11.1.2.2 software.

_Requirement:
Audio descriptions must be provided for all pre-recorded video content, when appropriate (see Note below). 

Audio description is additional audible narrative, inserted in natural pauses in the dialogue, which describes the significant aspects of the visual content of visual media that cannot be understood from the main soundtrack alone. It provides information about actions, characters, scene changes, on-screen text, and other visual content.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to pre-recorded video in audiovisual content published by Microsoft.

This requirement does not apply to:
- Third-party content that Microsoft licenses solely for redistribution, such as content provided via online streaming services. 
- Videos for which the significant aspects of the visual content can be understood from the main soundtrack alone. For example, a video of a company representative reading a press release, with no additional visual information shown such as photos or charts, does not require audio description. 
- Video players – See MAS 7.2, 7.3, 7.6, and 7.7 for rules applicable to video players. 
- Video creation and editing tools – See MAS 5.x for rules applicable to authoring tools.
_Guidance: MAS 1.2.5 - Audio Description (Pre-recorded) is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded) - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Audio-only and Video-only (Pre-recorded) to 9.1.2.5 web, 10.1.2.5 non-web documents, and 11.1.2.5 software.

_Requirement: Information, [structure](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-structure), and [relationships](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-relationships) conveyed through [presentation](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-presentation) can be [programmatically determined](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-programmatically-determinable) or are available in text.
_Applicability: This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.
_Guidance: MAS 1.3.1 - Info and Relationships is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Info and Relationships to 9.1.3.1 web, 10.1.3.1 non-web documents, and 11.1.3.1.1 software.

_DetectionPatterns: Text styled to visually appear as a heading but are not using heading elements or ARIA heading role attributes
Lists formatted visually but not using list markup
Tables lacking necessary column headers, row headers or both
Related content, such as form labels or descriptions, which are not programmatically associated
Custom ARIA markup patterns that contain invalid child elements

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Use appropriate semantic HTML elements to convey content structure. Use ARIA alternatives only when necessary
Examples: nav, main, header, footer, search, aside for important landmark elements

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Programmatically associate related content using ARIA attributes or HTML structures
Examples: aria-describedby for associating related visible information
aria-details for identifying related rich descriptive content that is not an immediate sibling to the element it details
fieldset/legend for groupings of related form controls
caption for providing tables accessible names

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Replace visual-only formatting with semantic markup
Examples: Convert text styled to appear as headings into actual headings
Update heading tags that were used for styling purposes to a more appropriate tag
Use list markup instead of line breaks and unicode bullets
Add table headers for data tables

ValidationCriteria: Content structure is programmatically determinable
Relationships between elements are clear
Information doesn't rely solely on visual presentation

Good: Proper heading hierarchy (h1, h2, h3)
Lists using ul, ol, and li elements
Data tables with th elements for row and column headers
Label element using for attribute to reference ID of the form control it labels
Bad: Fake headings using bold/large text
Lists created with line breaks instead of list elements
Tables without header cells
Form labels that are not associated with the control they are meant to label
Tooltips not being referenced with aria-describedby
Invalid nesting of content (button as direct child of UL element, link as direct child of element with role=row)

_Requirement: A [correct reading sequence](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-correct-reading-sequence) can be [programmatically determined](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-programmatically-determinable).
_Applicability: This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.
_Guidance: MAS 1.3.2 - Meaningful Sequence is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Meaningful Sequence to 9.1.3.2 web, 10.1.3.2 non-web documents, and 11.1.3.2.1 software.

_DetectionPatterns: Content order in DOM doesn't match visual presentation, resulting in the content order not being logical when read sequentially
CSS positioning that disrupts logical reading order
CSS flexbox or grid layouts that visually reorder content in a way that disrupts the logical reading order
Tabular data presented out of sequence, because it is not marked up as a table or grid
Multi-column layouts where the columns are meant to be read in a specific order, but the source order is not logical when linearized

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Arrange content in DOM/source order that matches the intended reading sequence
Examples: Match visual layout with markup order
Use CSS for visual positioning while maintaining logical source order
Ensure heading hierarchy follows document structure

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Use CSS positioning techniques that don't disrupt the logical reading order
Examples: CSS Grid and Flexbox with proper order
Avoid absolute positioning that breaks sequence
Test with CSS disabled to verify reading order

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Ensure complex layouts maintain meaningful sequence when linearized
Examples: Tangential content (e.g., sidebars) is placed after main content in source order

ValidationCriteria: Content can be read in a logical sequence
Source order matches intended reading flow
Information maintains meaning when CSS is disabled

Good: Source order matches visual layout left-to-right, top-to-bottom
Main content before sidebar in source order
Logical heading hierarchy (h1, h2, h3)
Bad: CSS grid or flexbox ordering that disrupts reading order
Using CSS absolute position to layout content in a way that doesn't match source order
Content using white space and visual markers such as '|' to create faux tables, but the content is not marked up as a table

_Requirement: Instructions provided for understanding and operating content do not rely solely on sensory characteristics of components such as shape, color, size, visual location, orientation, or sound.
_Applicability: This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.
_Guidance: MAS 1.3.3 - Sensory Characteristics is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.3.3 Sensory Characteristics - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Sensory Characteristics to 9.1.3.3 web, 10.1.3.3 non-web documents, and 11.1.3.3 software.

_Requirement:
Content does not restrict its view and operation to a single display orientation, such as portrait or landscape, unless a specific display orientation is [essential](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/orientation#dfn-essential).
Note: Examples where a particular display orientation may be essential are a bank check, a piano application, slides for a projector or television, or virtual reality content where content is not necessarily restricted to landscape or portrait display orientation.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to content that is only used on hardware with a fixed display orientation or that has no sensor to detect or change the orientation
_Guidance: MAS 1.3.4 - Orientation is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.3.4 Orientation - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Orientation to 9.1.3.4 web, 10.1.3.4 non-web documents, and 11.1.3.4 software.

_Requirement:
The purpose of each input field collecting information about the user can be programmatically determined when:
- The input field serves a purpose identified in the [Input Purposes for User Interface Components section](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/understanding/identify-input-purpose.html#input-purposes); and
- The content is implemented using technologies with support for identifying the expected meaning for form input data.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to software and electronic documents that do not provide attributes that support identifying the expected meaning for the form input data.
_Guidance: MAS 1.3.5 - Identify Input Purpose is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Identify Input Purpose to 9.1.3.5 web, 10.1.3.5 non-web documents, and 11.1.3.5.1 software.

_Requirement:
Color is not the sole means of communicating information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element.

Video: [EN 301 549 Use of Color](https://youtu.be/-Youn7nq9GY?t=17m6s)
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.

Note: This requirement addresses color perception specifically. Other forms of perception are covered in [Guideline 1.3](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#adaptable)  including programmatic access to color and other visual presentation coding.
_Guidance: MAS 1.4.1 - Use of Color is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.4.1 Use of Color - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Use of Color to 9.1.4.1 web, 10.1.4.1 non-web documents, and 11.1.4.1 software.

_DetectionPatterns: Information conveyed only through color differences
Links lacking underlines and relying on color alone to identify in blocks of text
Invalid form fields indicated only by red text (label, message or both) or border color
Required form fields vs optional form fields indicated by different label text colors
Chart data distinguished only by color
Status indicators using only color coding

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Provide additional non-color indicators alongside color coding
Use text, icons, or other visual cues in addition to color for status information
Examples: Error identifying text with red color

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Add patterns, labels, or other distinguishing features to color-coded data

ValidationCriteria: Information is available without color perception
All color-coded elements have non-color alternatives
Interface remains functional in grayscale
Where colors are used as unique identifiers, there is at least a 3:1 contrast ratio or greater between the colors

Good: Links within blocks of text are provided underlines as well as a color difference from static text
Error messages with both red color and error icon or explicit text that says 'error'
Required fields marked with asterisk (*) and red color
Charts using both color and patterns/symbols
Bad: Links lack an underline and do not have a 3:1 contrast difference compared to adjacent static text
Form errors shown only in red text and the text does not include the word 'error' or similar
Charts relying only on color coding
Status indicators using only color differences

_Requirement:
If any audio plays automatically for more than 3 seconds, either a  [mechanism](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-mechanism)  is available to pause or stop the audio, or a mechanism is available to control audio volume independently from the overall system volume level. 

Video: [EN 301 549 Audio Control](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1079&v=-Youn7nq9GY&feature=youtu.be)
_Applicability: This requirement applies to websites, software with a user interface, and electronic documents that support audio content.
_Guidance: MAS 1.4.2 - Audio Control is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.4.2 Audio Control - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Audio Control to 9.1.4.2 web, 10.1.4.2 non-web documents, and 11.1.4.2 software.

_Requirement:
Visible [text](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-text) must have a minimum luminosity [contrast ratio](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-contrast-ratio) of 4.5:1 against the background, except: - [Large-scale text](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-large-scale) (18 point or 14 point bold) and images of large-scale text must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1. - Text or [images of text](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-images-of-text) that are part of an inactive [user interface component](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-user-interface-components), that are [pure decoration](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-pure-decoration), that are not visible to anyone, or that are part of a picture that contains significant other visual content, have no contrast requirement. - Text that is part of a logo or brand name has no minimum contrast requirement.
Note: In the relative luminance formula, the value of 0.03928 comes from an outdated sRGB proposal. 0.04045 should be used in its place.
_Applicability: This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.
_Guidance: MAS 1.4.3 - Contrast (Minimum) is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Contrast Minimum to 9.1.4.3 web, 10.1.4.3 non-web documents, and 11.1.4.3 software.

_DetectionPatterns: Text with insufficient color contrast ratio
Normal text below 4.5:1 contrast ratio
Large text below 3:1 contrast ratio

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Adjust foreground or background colors to achieve minimum contrast ratios
Test with contrast analyzer tools and adjust until minimum ratios are met

ValidationCriteria: Normal text achieves 4.5:1 contrast ratio minimum
Large text achieves 3:1 contrast ratio minimum
Contrast maintained across different viewing conditions
Interactive element text contrast is below the minimum, but the interactive element is marked as disabled

Good: Black text on white background (21:1 ratio)
Dark blue (#003366) on white background (8.7:1 ratio)
White text on dark backgrounds with sufficient contrast
Low opacity text due to an interactive control being disabled
Bad: Light gray text on white backgrounds
Yellow text on white backgrounds
White text on orange backgrounds
Using only color differences without sufficient luminance contrast
Low opacity text due to an interactive control being disabled, but the control is still focusable or has some level of interactivity, e.g., it displays a tooltip on hover or focus

exceptions.description: Text or images of text that are part of inactive user interface components
Pure decoration, not visible to anyone, or part of pictures with significant other visual content
Text that is part of a logo or brand name

_Requirement:
[Text](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-text) can be resized without assistive technology up to 200% with no loss of content or functionality.  

Reference [Guideline 1.4.4 - Resize Text Resolution](https://microsoft.sharepoint.com/:w:/r/sites/accessibility/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7BB75CF91B-4D64-4408-9C2B-3359420D0D56%7D&file=Guideline%201.4.4%20%E2%80%93%20Resize%20Text%20Resolution.docx&action=default&mobileredirect=true&wdLOR=c38B87085-9A6E-4967-A1E9-79988BC4D143&cid=401c8dad-d537-4a5f-a4db-be0e25fd11f3&share=IQEb-Vy3ZE0IRJwrM1lCDQ1WAQihABcDGoOyLTGesAu9diE) provides  help for meeting this requirement.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface. 

The requirement does not apply to text that is [captions](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-captions) or [images of text](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-images-of-text).
_Guidance: MAS 1.4.4 -Resize Text is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.4.4 Resize Text - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Resize Text to 9.1.4.4 web, 10.1.4.4 non-web documents, and 11.1.4.4.1 software.

_Requirement: Text is used instead of images of text when technology allows, unless it is [essential](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-essential).
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.  

This requirement does not apply to logotypes (text that is part of a logo or brand name) or if the image of text can be  [visually customized](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-visually-customized)  to the user's requirements.
_Guidance: MAS 1.4.5 - Images of Text is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.4.5 Images of Text - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Images of Text to 9.1.4.5 web, 10.1.4.5 non-web documents, and 11.1.4.5.1 software.

_Requirement:
Content can be presented without loss of information or functionality, and without requiring scrolling in two dimensions for: - Vertical scrolling content at a width equivalent to 320 [CSS pixels](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-css-pixels); - Horizontal scrolling content at a height equivalent to 256 [CSS pixels](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-css-pixels);

Except for parts of the content which require two-dimensional layout for usage or meaning.

Note: 320 CSS pixels is equivalent to a starting viewport width of 1280 CSS pixels wide at 400% zoom. For web content which is designed to scroll horizontally (e.g., with vertical text), 256 CSS pixels is equivalent to a starting viewport height of 1024 CSS pixels at 400% zoom. Note: Examples of content which requires two-dimensional layout are images required for understanding (such as maps and diagrams), video, games, presentations, data tables (not individual cells), and interfaces where it is necessary to keep toolbars in view while manipulating content. It is acceptable to provide two-dimensional scrolling for such parts of the content.
_Applicability: This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.
_Guidance: MAS 1.4.10 - Reflow is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.4.10 Reflow - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Reflow to 9.1.4.10 web, 10.1.4.10 non-web documents, and 11.1.4.10 software.

_Requirement:
The visual [presentation](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-presentation) of the following have a [contrast ratio](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-contrast-ratio) of at least 3:1 against adjacent color(s)

- **User Interface Components:**
Visual information used to indicate [states](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-states) and boundaries of [user interface components](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-user-interface-components), except for inactive components or where the appearance of the component is determined by the user agent or platform software and not modified by the author. Any visual information necessary to indicate state, such as whether a component is selected or focused must also ensure that the information used to identify the control in that state has a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio.
	- This does not require that changes in color that differentiate between states of an individual component meet the 3:1 contrast ratio when they do not appear next to each other. For example, there is not a new requirement that visited links contrast with the default color, or that mouse hover indicators contrast with the default state. However, the component must not lose contrast with the adjacent colors, and non-text indicators such as the check in a checkbox or an arrow graphic indicating a menu is selected or open must have sufficient contrast to the adjacent colors.
	- This does not require that controls have a visual boundary indicating the hit area, but if the visual indicator of the control is the only way to identify the control, then that indicator must have sufficient contrast. If text (or an icon) within a button or placeholder text inside a text input is visible and there is no visual indication of the hit area then the requirement is met. If a button with text also has a colored border, since the border does not provide the only indication there is no contrast requirement beyond the text contrast (1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)). Note that for people with cognitive disabilities it is recommended to delineate the boundary of controls to aid in the recognition of controls and therefore the completion of activities.

- **Graphical Objects:** </br>
Parts of graphics required to understand the content, except when a particular presentation of graphics is [essential](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-essential) to the information being conveyed.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply in the following situations: 

**User Interface Components:**
inactive components or where the appearance of the component is determined by the user agent or platform software and not modified by the author.

_Requirement:
Where receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, the following are true: - **Dismissible:** A [mechanism](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-mechanism) is available to dismiss the additional content without moving pointer hover or keyboard focus, unless the additional content communicates an [input error](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-input-error) or does not obscure or replace other content.

- **Hoverable:** If pointer hover can trigger the additional content, then the pointer can be moved over the additional content without the additional content disappearing. - **Persistent:** The additional content remains visible until the hover or focus trigger is removed, the user dismisses it, or its information is no longer valid.
Exception: The visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the user agent or platform software and is not modified by the author.
Note: Examples of additional content controlled by the user agent or platform software include tooltips created through use of the HTML [title attribute](https://www.w3.org/TR/html/dom.html#the-title-attribute) or user interface object attributes.
Note: Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other nonmodal popups that display on hover and focus are examples of additional content covered by this criterion.
Note: This criterion applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering component itself. Since hidden components that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this criterion.
_Applicability: This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface
_Guidance: MAS 1.4.13 - Content on Hover or Focus is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Content on Hover or Focus to 9.1.4.13 web, 10.1.4.13 non-web documents, and 11.1.4.13 software.

Allow pointer to move over additional content without it disappearing
Examples: Maintain popup when hovering over its content
Provide connection between trigger and popup

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Keep additional content visible until trigger is removed or user dismisses it

ValidationCriteria: Additional content can be dismissed without removing trigger

_Requirement:
If a [keyboard shortcut](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-keyboard-shortcuts) is implemented in content using only letter (including upper- and lower-case letters), punctuation, number, or symbol characters, then at least one of the following is true. - **Turn off:** A [mechanism](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-mechanism) is available to turn off the shortcut. - **Remap:** A mechanism is available to remap the shortcut to use one or more non-printable keyboard characters (e.g. Ctrl, Alt, et cetera). - **Active only on focus:** The keyboard shortcut for a [user interface component](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-user-interface-components) is only active when that component has focus.
NOTE: A long press of a key (2 seconds or more) and other accessibility features provided by the platform do not meet the [definition of a keyboard shortcut](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag2ict-22/#dfn-keyboard-shortcut).
_Applicability: This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.

_Requirement:
For any feature that requires users to complete an action within a set period of time, at least one of the following is true:
- **Turn off:** The user is allowed to turn off the time limit before encountering it; OR - **Adjust:** The user is allowed to adjust the time limit before encountering it over a wide range that is at least ten times the length of the default setting; OR - **Extend:** The user is warned before time expires and given at least 20 seconds to extend the time limit with a simple action (for example, "press the space bar"), and the user is allowed to extend the time limit at least ten times; OR - **Real-time:** The time limit is a required part of a real-time event (for example, gameplay or a live auction), and no alternative to the time limit is possible; OR - **Essential:** The time limit is essential and extending it would invalidate the activity; OR - **20 Hour:** The time limit is longer than 20 hours.
_Applicability: This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.
_Guidance: MAS 2.2.1 - Timing Adjustable is based on these standards: - WCAG: 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Timing Adjustable to 9.2.2.1 web, 10.2.2.1 non-web documents, and 11.2.2.1 software.

_Requirement:
Any auto-updating content that starts automatically and is provided with other content provides a method for users to pause, stop, hide, or to control the frequency of the update. 

Any moving, blinking or scrolling information that starts automatically, lasts for more than five seconds, and is presented with other content, provides a method for users to pause, stop, or hide it. 

Note: For requirements related to flickering or flashing content, refer to [Guideline 2.3](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#seizures-and-physical-reactions).
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface

This requirement does not apply if the moving, blinking, scrolling, or auto-updating information is part of an activity where it is [essential](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-essential).

_Requirement:
Expose visual groupings and semantic structure of controls and content programmatically so that users can identify and navigate to, or through, them. Additionally, provide ways for users to activate, or navigate directly to, controls and content with as few interactions as possible (for example, bypass UI elements by using keyboard shortcuts or “link to content” links). 

Note: While the user of headings and landmarks are sufficient techniques to provide bypass blocks for people who use assistive technologies, there are no mainstream user agents (browsers) that allow for this functionality without the use of assistive technologies or additional plug-ins. For this reason, for web pages, another mechanism must be provided to allow users who primarily use keyboard to navigate the web, to bypass globally repeating content. For instance, a skip to main content link is a common feature used to allow quick navigation past globally repeating content of a website’s header and navigation area.
_Applicability: This requirement applies to websites.

_DetectionPatterns: Form fields without labels or instructions
Required fields not clearly marked
Complex input formats without examples or guidance
Error-prone fields without preventive instructions

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Provide clear labels for all form inputs using label elements or ARIA attributes
Add helpful instructions for complex or formatted inputs
Clearly indicate required fields and any special formatting needs

ValidationCriteria: All form inputs have associated labels
Required fields are clearly marked
Complex input formats include examples or instructions

Good: Label element: <label for='email'>Email Address *</label>
Format instruction: 'Phone Number (xxx-xxx-xxxx)'
Required field indicator: 'Password * (minimum 8 characters)'

Placeholder text as only label

_Requirement: For all detected [input errors](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-input-error) – after identifying the location where the error occurred and describing the error in text – provide users with actionable suggestions for correcting it, unless it would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.

_Requirement:
For websites, electronic documents, and software that cause  [legal commitments](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-legal-commitments) or financial transactions for the user to occur, that modify or delete [user-controllable](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-user-controllable) data in data storage systems, or that submit user test responses, at least one of the following is true:

**Reversible:** Submissions are reversible.

**Checked:** Data entered by the user is checked for input errors and the user is provided an opportunity to correct them.

**Confirmed:** A mechanism is available for reviewing, confirming, and correcting information before finalizing the submission.
_Applicability: This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.

_Requirement:

_Requirement: For all [user interface components](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-user-interface-components) (including but not limited to: form elements, links and components generated by scripts), the [name](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-name) and [role](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-role) can be [programmatically determined](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-programmatically-determinable); states, properties, and values that can be set by the user can be [programmatically set](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-programmatically-set); and notification of changes to these items is available to [user agents](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-user-agents), including [assistive technologies](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#dfn-assistive-technologies). For any website, product, service, tool, or content, functionality and navigation of the content and user interface components must be programmatically exposed and operable.
_Applicability: This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.
_Guidance: MAS 4.1.2 - Name, Role, Value is based on these standards: - WCAG: 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Name, Role, Value to 9.4.1.2 web, 10.4.1.2 non-web documents, and 11.4.1.2.1 software.

_DetectionPatterns: Interactive elements without accessible names
Custom components missing ARIA roles
Form controls without proper labels
Invalid nesting of interactive elements within other interactive elements
Misuse of aria-hidden on elements that contain focusable elements, or are already hidden with CSS display: none or visibility: hidden
Dynamic content changes not announced to assistive technology

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Provide accessible names for all interactive elements using labels, the element's text content, or ARIA attributes. ARIA attributes should only be used as a last resort when other methods are not feasible.
Examples: provide visible text within a button or link to name it
alt text for images within buttons and links
aria-labelledby for elements with visible text labels that can't use the label element
use aria-label to name elements that don't have visible text labels or already use other naming techniques

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Accessible names should not be provided to generic elements (e.g., divs or spans) or elements with roles that ARIA prohibits from having an accessible name.
Examples: remove aria-label from generic div elements, or provide the div with an appropriate ARIA role that allows it to have an accessible name

do not use aria-label or aria-labelledby on label elements. Instead, if a form control needs an accessible name that has more information than what is present in the visible label, then use aria-describedby to provide additional information about the form control

if an element has role=none or role=presentation, remove any aria-label or aria-labelledby attributes from the element. An element can't be marked as presentational and also provided an accessible name
do not use aria-label to repeat the visible text of a control, exactly

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Use the appropriate native HTML element, or define appropriate ARIA roles for custom components to communicate their purpose. Prioritize using native HTML over ARIA whenever possible.
Examples: use the button element, or role='button' for custom buttons
use the nav element or role='navigation' for nav areas
use the dialog element or role='dialog' for modal dialogs

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Communicate component states and properties using the appropriate HTML or ARIA attributes. Do not use both native HTML attributes and ARIA attribute counterparts for the same state or property, as this could result in conflicts. Prioritize using native HTML attributes over ARIA whenever possible.
Examples: the checked attribute for native checkboxes or aria-checked for custom ARIA checkboxes
the disabled attribute or aria-disabled for inactive elements

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Use aria-hidden=true to hide content from assistive technologies only when the content is still visually present. If content is hidden from all users, use CSS display: none or visibility: hidden instead. If using aria-hidden=true to hide content from assistive technologies, ensure that the content does not contain focusable elements, as this can result in inaccessible content.
Examples: if content is hidden from all users, use display: none or visibility: hidden instead of aria-hidden=true

if using aria-hidden=true to hide content from assistive technologies, if there are focusable elements within the aria-hidden=true container, either ensure they are set to disabled or have been removed from the document focus order (e.g., with tabindex=-1)
if content is meant to be inert, use the inert attribute instead of using aria-hidden=true and attempting to ensure focusable content cannot be focused
do not use inert for elements that should be marked as disabled

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Elements with interactive roles (widts) should not be nested within other interactive elements, as this can result in the name, role and value/state of the nested element or its parent being incorrectly exposed, or completely inaccessible.
Examples: a button cannot be specified within a button, option, menuitem, etc.
links cannot contain other interactive elements
if a design calls for what appears to be interactive elements, make sure the elements are instead siblings, and use CSS to position the elements to appear as if they are nested, when necessary

ValidationCriteria: Interactive elements must never be nested within other elements with interactive roles
All interactive elements have accessible names
Component roles are properly defined or the native HTML equivalent is used
States and properties are programmatically available
Focusable elements cannot be accessed if they are within an aria-hidden=true container element

Good: Form inputs with associated label elements
Buttons with descriptive text or aria-label if visible text is not present
Custom components with the required ARIA roles and properties
Use display: none or visibility: hidden instead of aria-hidden=true to hide content from assistive technologies when the content is also visually hidden
Bad: Buttons visually presented with only an icon and no text or aria-label
aria-labels that repeat the same text as visible content
title attributes that repeat the same text as the aria-label or visible text content
interactive elements that have nested interactive elements within them
Form inputs without associated labels
Using aria-hidden=true when an element is already set to display: none or visibility: hidden
Interactive elements or components without ARIA roles
Interactive elements with non-interactive roles, but with aria-roledescription that falsifies the role of the element. E.g., a div with role='group' and aria-roledescription='button'

_Requirement: In content implemented using markup languages or that supports status message notifications, [status messages](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-status-messages) can be [programmatically determined](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-programmatically-determinable) through [role](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-role) or properties such that they can be presented to the user by [assistive technologies](https://w3c.github.io/wcag21/guidelines/#dfn-assistive-technologies) without receiving focus.
_Applicability: This requirement applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.
_Guidance: MAS 4.1.3 - Status Messages is based on these standards: - WCAG: 4.1.3 Status Messages - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Status Messages to 9.4.1.3 web, 10.4.1.3 non-web documents, and 11.4.1.3.1 software.

_Requirement:
**Software with a user interface:** The object role, state(s), properties, boundary, name, and description must be programmatically determinable. Where the platform provides accessibility APIs (for example, UIA on Windows) the object, role, state(s), properties, boundary, name and description must be provided to the accessibility API. 

**Platforms:** Platform APIs must enable software with a user interface to make object role, state(s), properties, boundary, name, and description programmatically determinable.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to platforms and all software with a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to websites.
_Guidance: MAS 4.2.1 - Object Information is based on these standards: - Section 508: 502.3.1 Object Information. - EN 301 549: 11.5.2.5 Object information (PDF).

_Requirement:
**Software with a user interface:** States and properties that can be set by the user must be capable of being set programmatically via the platform APIs. 

**Platforms:** Platform APIs must enable assistive technology to set states and properties that can be set by the user.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to platforms and all software with a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to websites.
_Guidance: MAS 4.2.2 - Modifications of States and Properties is based on these standards: - Section 508: 502.3.2 Modification of Object Information. - EN 301 549: 11.5.2.16 Modifications of states and properties (PDF).

_Requirement:
**Software with a user interface:** If an object is in a data table, the occupied rows and columns, and any headers associated with those rows or columns, must be programmatically determinable. Where the platform provides accessibility APIs (for example, UIA on Windows) and the object is in a data table, the occupied rows and columns, and any headers associated with those rows or columns must be provided to the accessibility API. 

**Platforms:** Platform APIs must enable software with a user interface to make row and column headers of data tables programmatically determinable.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to platforms and all software with a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to websites.
_Guidance: MAS 4.2.3 - Row, Column, and Headers is based on these standards: - Section 508: 502.3.3 Row, Column and Headers. - EN 301 549: 11.5.2.6 Row, column, and headers (PDF).

_Requirement:
**Software with a user interface:** Any current value(s), and any set or range of allowable values associated with an object, must be programmatically determinable. Where the platform provides accessibility APIs (for example, UIA on Windows) any current value(s), and any set or range of allowable values associated with an object must be provided to the accessibility API. 

**Platforms:** Platform APIs must enable software with a user interface to provide any current value(s) and any set or range of allowable values associated with an object, making them programmatically determinable.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to platforms and all software with a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to websites.
_Guidance: MAS 4.2.4 - Values is based on these standards: - Section 508: 502.3.4 Values. - EN 301 549: 11.5.2.7 Values (PDF).

_Requirement:
**Software with a user interface:** Any relationship that a component has as a label for another component, or of being labeled by another component, must be programmatically determinable. Where the platform provides accessibility APIs (for example, UIA on Windows) the object, role, state(s), properties, boundary, name and description must be provided to the accessibility API. 

 

**Platforms:** Platform APIs must enable software with a user interface to provide any relationship that a component has as a label for another component, or of being labeled by another component, the object, role, state(s), properties, boundary, name and description, making them programmatically determinable.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to platforms and all software with a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to websites.
_Guidance: MAS 4.2.5 - Label Relationships is based on these standards: - Section 508: 502.3.6 Label Relationships. - EN 301 549: 11.5.2.8 Label relationships (PDF).

_Requirement:
**Software with a user interface:** Any hierarchical (parent-child) relationship that a component has as a container for, or being contained by, another component must be programmatically determinable. Where the platform provides accessibility APIs (for example, UIA on Windows) the parent-child relationship must be provided to the accessibility API.

**Platforms:** Platform APIs must enable software with a user interface to provide any hierarchical (parent-child) relationship that a component has as a container for, or being contained by, another component, making them programmatically determinable.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to platforms and all software with a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to websites.
_Guidance: MAS 4.2.6 - Parent-Child Relationships is based on these standards: - Section 508: 502.3.7 Hierarchical Relationships. - EN 301 549: 11.5.2.9 Parent-child relationships (PDF).

_Requirement:
**Software with a user interface:** The content of text objects, text attributes, and the boundary of text rendered to the screen, must be programmatically determinable. Where the platform provides accessibility APIs (for example, UIA on Windows) the content of text objects, text attributes, and the boundary of text rendered to the screen must be provided to the accessibility API. 


**Platforms:** Platform APIs must enable software with a user interface to provide the content of text objects, text attributes, and the boundary of text rendered to the screen, making them programmatically determinable.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to platforms and all software with a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to websites.
_Guidance: MAS 4.2.7 - Text is based on these standards: - Section 508: 502.3.8 Text. - EN 301 549: 11.5.2.10 Text (PDF).

_Requirement:
**Software with a user interface:** A list of all actions that can be executed on an object must be programmatically determinable. Where the platform provides accessibility APIs (for example, UIA on Windows) A list of all actions that can be executed on an object must be provided to the accessibility API. 

**Platforms:** Platform APIs must enable software with a user interface to provide a list of all actions that can be executed on an object, making them programmatically determinable.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to platforms and all software with a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to websites.
_Guidance: MAS 4.2.8 - List of Available Actions is based on these standards: - Section 508: 502.3.10 List of Actions. - EN 301 549: 11.5.2.11 List of available actions (PDF).

_Requirement:
**Software with a user interface:** Applications must allow assistive technology to programmatically execute available actions on objects using platform accessibility APIs. 

 

**Platforms:** Platform APIs must enable assistive technology to execute available actions on objects.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to platforms and all software with a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to websites.
_Guidance: MAS 4.2.9 - Execution of Available Actions is based on these standards: - Section 508: 502.3.11 Action on Objects. - EN 301 549: 11.5.2.12 Execution of available actions (PDF).

_Title: Tracking of Focus and Selection Attributes
_Requirement:
**Software with a user interface:** Applications must expose information and mechanisms necessary to track focus, text insertion point, and selection attributes of user interface components (for example, whether text has been selected for copy/paste). Where the platform provides accessibility APIs (for example, UIA on Windows) the information and mechanisms necessary to track focus, text insertion point, and selection attributes of user interface components must be provided to the accessibility APIs. 

 

**Platforms:** Platform APIs must enable software with a user interface to provide information and mechanisms necessary to track focus, text insertion point, and selection attributes of user interface components, making them programmatically determinable.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to platforms and all software with a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to websites.
_Guidance: MAS 4.2.10 - Tracking of Focus and Selection Attributes is based on these standards: - Section 508: 502.3.12 Focus Cursor. - EN 301 549: 11.5.2.13 Tracking of focus and selection attributes (PDF).

_Title: Modification of Focus and Selection Attributes
_Requirement:
**Software with a user interface:** Focus, text insertion point, and selection attributes (for example, whether text has been selected for copy/paste) that can be set by the user must be capable of being set programmatically, including through the use of assistive technology, via platform APIs. 

**Platforms:** Platform APIs must enable assistive technology to set focus, text insertion point, and selection attributes (for example, whether text has been selected for copy/paste) that can be set by the user.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to platforms and all software with a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to websites.
_Guidance: MAS 4.2.11 - Modification of Focus and Selection Attributes is based on these standards: - Section 508: 502.3.13 Modification of Focus Cursor. - EN 301 549: 11.5.2.14 Modification of focus and selection attributes (PDF).

_Requirement:
**Software with a user interface:** Notification of events relevant to user interactions, including but not limited to changes in the component's state(s), value, name, description, or boundary, must be available to assistive technology via the accessibility APIs (e.g. UIA on Windows). 

**Platforms:** Platform APIs must enable software with a user interface to provide notification of events relevant to user interactions, including but not limited to changes in the component's state(s), value, name, description, or boundary, making them programmatically determinable.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to platforms and all software with a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to websites.
_Guidance: MAS 4.2.12 - Change Notification is based on these standards: - Section 508: 502.3.14 Event Notification. - EN 301 549: 11.5.2.15 Change notification (PDF).

_Requirement:
**Software with a user interface:** When permitted by security requirements, software that provides a user interface must, by using platform APIs (for example, UIA on Windows), allow assistive technologies to modify values and text of user interface elements using the input methods of the platform, if the values and text of these elements can be modified by users without assistive technology. 

**Platforms:** Platform APIs must enable assistive technology to modify values and text of user interface elements that can be modified by the user
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to platforms and all software with a user interface. 

This requirement does not apply to websites.
_Guidance: MAS 4.2.13 - Modifications of Values and Text is based on these standards: - Section 508: 502.3.5 Modification of Values. - Section 508: 502.3.9 Modification of Text. - EN 301 549: 11.5.2.17 Modifications of values and text (PDF).

_Requirement:
Software with a user interface must interoperate with and not disrupt documented accessibility features that are defined in platform documentation, except when requested to do so by the user during the operation of the software.  
Note: This will often be achieved by coding to the Platform Accessibility APIs - see [MAS 4.2.1-4.2.13](https://microsoft.sharepoint.com/teams/msenable/mas/Pages/default.aspx).

For Windows, “Accessibility features” are defined as those found in the Windows Accessibility Settings
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to any software with a user interface. 

Microsoft also applies this requirement to websites, although not included in the underlying web standards.
_Guidance: MAS 4.3.1 - No Disruption of Accessibility Features is based on these standards: - Section 508: 502.2.2 No Disruption of Accessibility Features. - EN 301 549: 11.6.2 No disruption of accessibility features (PDF).

_Requirement:
Where an application provides an alternative user interface that functions as assistive technology, the application must use platform and other industry standard accessibility services. 

Note: This MAS will rarely apply; such alternative interfaces or unique assistive technologies are rarely created by engineering teams.
_Applicability: This requirement applies to any software with a user interface.
_Guidance: MAS 4.3.2 - Alternative User Interfaces is based on these standards: - Section 508: 503.3 Alternative User Interfaces.

_Requirement:
Authoring tools must enable users to create or edit applications, services, tools, and content that is accessible. Authoring tools shall permit authors the option of overriding information required for accessibility.

Notes: • Authoring tools may rely on additional tools to create accessible content **only if** it is not achievable (i.e., technically possible) in a single tool. • For video creation and editing tools, this requirement includes supporting the creation and editing of videos with closed captions and audio descriptions. • This requirement includes enabling users to edit video captions and transcripts created using automatic speech recognition for accuracy.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to authoring tools. An authoring tool is any software that can be used by authors, alone or collaboratively, to create or modify content or to develop applications or services, for use by other people (other authors or end users). Notes: • “Content” includes documents, websites, blogs, images, video, and user-generated content. • Any software that offers an ability for authors or end users to create rich text content is considered an authoring tool. • Any software that **only** offers an ability for authors or end users to create plain text content is **not** considered an authoring tool.
This requirement does not apply when the authoring tool is used to directly edit plain text or plain text source code.
_Guidance: MAS 5.1 - Accessible Content Creation is based on these standards: - Section 508: 504.2 Content Creation or Editing. - EN 301 549: 11.8.2 Accessible Content Creation (PDF).
AdditionalInformation: W3C Authoring Tool Accessibility Guidelines (ATAG) 2.0 The Authoring Tool Accessibility Guidelines (ATAG) 2.0 provides guidelines for designing web content authoring tools that are both more accessible to authors with disabilities (Part A) and designed to enable, support, and promote the production of more accessible web content by all authors (Part B). See [Authoring Tool Accessibility Guidelines (ATAG) Overview](http://www.w3.org/WAI/intro/atag.php)

_Title: Preservation of Accessibility Information in Transformations
_Requirement: When converting content from one format to another or saving content in multiple formats, authoring tools must preserve the information required for accessibility to the extent that the information is supported by the destination format.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to authoring tools that support converting content from one format to another or saving content in multiple formats. An authoring tool is *any software that can be used by authors, alone or collaboratively, to create or modify content or to develop applications or services, for use by other people (other authors or end users).*

Notes:
- “Content” includes documents, websites, blogs, images, video, and user-generated content.
- Any software that offers an ability for authors or end users to create rich text content is considered an authoring tool.
- Any software that **only** offers an ability for authors or end users to create plain text content is **not** considered an authoring tool.
_Guidance: MAS 5.2 - Preservation of Accessibility Information in Transformations is based on these standards: - Section 508: 504.2.1 Preservation of Information Provided for Accessibility in Format Conversion. - EN 301 549: 11.8.3 Preservation of accessibility information in transformations (PDF).

_Requirement:
Authoring tools that provide a mechanism for authors to check content for accessibility problems must provide repair suggestions. 

Note: If an authoring tool does not provide a mechanism for authors to check content for accessibility problems, one does not need to be added to meet this requirement.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to authoring tools that include a mechanism for authors to check content for accessibility problems. An authoring tool is any software that can be used by authors, alone or collaboratively, to create or modify content or to develop applications or services, for use by other people (other authors or end users). 

Notes:  
- “Content” includes documents, websites, blogs, images, video, and user-generated content. 
- Any software that offers an ability for authors or end users to create rich text content is considered an authoring tool. 
- Any software that **only** offers an ability for authors or end users to create plain text content is **not** considered an authoring tool.
_Guidance: MAS 5.3 - Repair Assistance is based on these standards: - EN 301 549: 11.8.4 Repair assistance (PDF).
AdditionalInformation: The Authoring Tool Accessibility Guidelines (ATAG) 2.0 provides guidelines for designing web content authoring tools that are both more accessible to authors with disabilities (Part A) and designed to enable, support, and promote the production of more accessible web content by all authors (Part B). See [Authoring Tool Accessibility Guidelines (ATAG) Overview.](https://w3c.github.io/wai-website/standards-guidelines/atag/#main)

_Requirement:
Anything that provides two-way voice communication must be able to encode and decode speech in a frequency rangeup to at least 7000 Hz and must either (1) transmit and receive speech that is digitally encoded in the manner specified by [ITU-T G.722.2](http://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-G.722.2/en) or [IETF 6716](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6716); or (2) use an alternate codec that results in an equal or superior audio quality for the end user as would be obtained using ITU-T G.722.2 or IETF 6716.

Note: If option (2) is utilized, customer conformance statements relating to this requirement should explain in the "remarks and explanation" field that we use technology that meets or exceeds the audio quality provided by and G.722.2 / IETF RFC 6716.
_Applicability: This requirement applies to anything that provides two-way voice communication.

_Requirement:
Real-Time Text (RTT) means text communications that are transmitted over IP networks immediately as they are created ( on a character-by-character basis). The text is sent immediately without the user needing to hit “send”.   

**European Union:** Under EU law, anything that provides two-way voice communication must also provide RTT for point to point and multi-party calls. The technical specifications of EN 301 549 listed in the Standards section should be followed to meet this requirement but note that the definition of RTT in EU law differs from EN 301 549 in that the law explicitly requires the text to be sent on a character-by-character basis. ETSI Technical Report (TR) 103 708 “Real-Time Text in Multiparty Conference Calling” provides guidance for implementing multi-party RTT. 

**United States and Canada:** Under U.S. and Canadian law, mobile handsets and other devices for use with IP-based voice services from wireless service providers must provide RTT. Because wireless service providers define the technical implementations of RTT, individual service provider device specifications should be consulted to determine detailed engineering requirements.
_Applicability:
**European Union:** This requirement applies to anything that provides two-way voice communication. 

**United States and Canada:** This requirement applies to mobile handsets and other devices for use with IP-based voice services from wireless service providers.

_Title: Requirements for Voice Mail, Auto Attendants, and IVR
_Requirement:
Anything that provide two-way voice communication and also provide voice mail, auto-attendant, or interactive voice response (IVR) must offer users a means to access the information and carry out tasks without the use of hearing or speech. Where provided, voice mail, auto-attendant, interactive voice response, and caller identification systemsmust be usable with a TTY. 

Note: Tasks that involve both operating the interface and perceiving the information would require that both the interface and information be accessible without use of speech or hearing. 

Additionally, voicemail, IVR systems, and related telecommunication functions that provide playback must include player controls that allow users to pause, skip, rewind, and repeat all messages and prompts.
_Applicability: This requirement applies to anything that provides two-way voice communication and voicemail, auto-attendant, or interactive voice response (IVR).

_Requirement:
Devices that include a voice cellular antenna and Voice over IP (VoIP) services that are interconnected with the PSTN that do not provide built-in TTY functionality must provide the following: 

- **TTY connectability:** provide a standard non-acoustic connection point for TTYs. 

- **Voice and Hearing Carry Over:** provide a microphone capable of being easily turned on and off to allow the user to intermix speech with TTY use. 

- **Signal Compatibility:** support all commonly used cross-manufacturer non-proprietary standard TTY signal protocols where the system interoperates with the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN).
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to: 

- Devices that include a voice cellular antenna  

- Voice over IP (VoIP) services that are interconnected with the PSTN

_Title: User Interfaces, Video Programming Guides and Menus
_Requirement:
Any user interface that a person must navigate in order to launch applications that play video programming must be accompanied by audio output (such as through a screen reader). The following functions, if offered through an onscreen text menu, must be accompanied by audible output: 
1.	Power on / off
2.	Volume adjust / mute
3.	Channel / program selection (including on-demand programming)
4.	Display channel / program information (including on-demand programming)
5.	Configuration / set-up (for example, language selection, parental controls)
6.	Enable / disable closed captioning 
7.	Configuration of closed captioning options (for example, changing font size, color) 
8.	Enable / disable video description  
9.	Display configuration info 
10.	Playback functions (for example, play, pause, rewind, fast forward, stop, and record) 
11.	Input selection.

Covered devices and applications are not required to include any or all of these functions, but if they are included, they must be accessible. 

If any of these 11 functions are offered other than through on-screen menus (for example, power-on functionality could be activated via the hardware) then those functions must still be accessible for individuals without vision, with low vision and limited or no hearing, and with limited or no color perception. 

A feature is "accessible" if the input, control, and mechanical functions are locatable, identifiable, and operable for a person with a disability. A person with a disability should have at least one method for using the feature that provides equivalent functionality as is available to users without a disability. For example, the power-on mechanical control should be tactilely discernable to aid use by individuals with visual impairments; patterns should be used to augment color cues for those with limited color perception.
_Applicability:
This requirement applies to: 

- Devices that receive or playback video programming 
- Devices with preinstalled video applications 
- Video applications that Microsoft directs people to use to access video programming 

If those devices have 

- Onscreen menus that offer any of 11 specific video playback functions, or 
- Offer video playback functionality in a manner other than onscreen text menus, such as a power on/off on hardware. 

The FCC defines “video programming” as “programming provided by, or generally considered comparable to programming provided by, a television broadcast station, but not including consumer-generated media.” 

This requirement does not apply to video communications (See the MAS 6.6 series for applicable requirements.)
_Guidance: MAS 7.6 – User Interfaces, Video Programming Guides and Menus is based on these regulations: - FCC: 47 CFR §79.107(a) User interfaces provided by digital apparatus

_Title: Secondary Audio Stream Support for Recording Devices and Video Players that Support Linear Programming

_Applicability:

Linear programming is prescheduled broadcast programming delivered via cable, satellite, or over the air. Linear programming does not include on-demand programming. 

This requirement does not apply to video communications (See the MAS 6.6 series for applicable requirements.)

_Requirement:

If you are designing a mobile handset, please reach out immediately to the Accessibility Technical Team [accTT@microsoft.com]("mailto:accTT@microsoft.com") for detailed requirements.

_Title: Hearing Aid Compatibility (HAC) for Mobile Handsets (M mode)
_Requirement:
